newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia moves to create gold market.
newsitem.headline: Russia moves to create gold market.

text.p: Russia has taken steps to create a gold market by freeing the prices at which domestic commercial banks may buy and sell bullion and by preparing to allow banks to export precious metals, the central bank said on Wednesday.
Sergei Kyshtymov, head of the Central Bank of Russia's precious metals directorate, told a briefing the bank began quoting gold, silver and platinum prices on Wednesday based on London evening fixes.
A central bank statement said commercial banks could not trade in platinum, and Russia's prices for the white metal would be for deals between the central bank and the government.
Kyshtymov also said the bank would sign a document next week authorising commercial banks with special licences to export gold and silver under certain conditions.
But exports of gold via commercial banks would cost more than those through the central bank, he said, possibly referring to tariffs and duties.
Commercial banks are estimated to hold a mere five tonnes of gold, which is only about four percent of Russia's output last year of around 124 tonnes.

The new trading rules cover deals between certain commercial banks and the central bank. Private citizens were recently allowed to buy and sell very small amounts of gold domestically, but other entities may not trade precious metals commercially.

Only a select number of domestic commercial banks may trade in precious metals at the newly liberalised prices, with the central bank controlling supply. The minimum size of operations was set at 60 kg for gold and one tonne for silver.
Kyshtymov said central bank bids would be London evening fixes minus two percent and offers would be at the fix plus two percent.

Russia was the world's fifth largest gold producer last year and has the world's third largest unmined reserves. Moscow is hoping to get commercial banks to lend money to mines to finance output, but restrictions on exports have hurt those plans.
Some analysts have questioned the extent to which the central bank's changes will create a market, since the bank has said it plans to buy most domestic output to increase its reserves.
